plan.contextChunk: This figure is a line graph of four straight lines tracing free energy against temperature for the four sign combinations of enthalpy and entropy change. The vertical axis is labeled Free energy and the horizontal axis Increasing temperature (K); the only numeral shown is 0 on the vertical axis. A gray dashed line at that zero splits the field into a pink upper half labeled Nonspontaneous, with delta G greater than 0 printed beside the axis, and a green lower half labeled Spontaneous, with delta G less than 0. All four lines start at the left edge. A red line begins high in the pink field and climbs to the upper right, labeled delta H greater than 0, delta S less than 0, while a green line begins in the green field and falls to the lower right, labeled delta H less than 0, delta S greater than 0. Two yellow lines lie between them and both cross the dashed zero line: one starts in the pink field and slopes downward, labeled delta H greater than 0, delta S greater than 0, the other starts in the green field and slopes upward, labeled delta H less than 0, delta S less than 0. Starting half and slope sign together encode the two arithmetic signs, so only the yellow pair changes shading as temperature rises, each at its own x-intercept. The plot motivates why a process whose enthalpy and entropy changes share a sign reverses spontaneity at the temperature where free energy is zero.

interactionPlan.concept: The sign of ΔG = ΔH − TΔS determines spontaneity, so ΔH sets the starting side of the plot while ΔS controls whether increasing temperature raises or lowers ΔG.

demo_steps.title: Read the zero boundary
demo_steps.narration: The dashed horizontal line is ΔG = 0. Points above it are nonspontaneous, while points below it are spontaneous.

demo_steps.title: Temperature always matters through the slope
demo_steps.narration: Drag the temperature cursor: each highlighted point moves along its line according to ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. Lines that never cross zero remain always spontaneous or always nonspontaneous.

demo_steps.title: Opposite signs: always nonspontaneous
demo_steps.narration: For ΔH > 0 and ΔS < 0, the process starts above zero and the slope is upward, so increasing temperature only makes ΔG more positive.

demo_steps.title: Opposite signs: always spontaneous
demo_steps.narration: For ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0, the process starts below zero and the slope is downward, so increasing temperature only makes ΔG more negative.

demo_steps.title: Same positive signs: spontaneous only at high temperature
demo_steps.narration: For ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0, the line starts nonspontaneous but slopes downward. Once the temperature cursor passes the ΔG = 0 intercept, the process becomes spontaneous.

demo_steps.title: Same negative signs: spontaneous only at low temperature
demo_steps.narration: For ΔH < 0 and ΔS < 0, the line starts spontaneous but slopes upward. At sufficiently high temperature it crosses into the nonspontaneous region.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Only when ΔH and ΔS have the same sign can temperature reverse spontaneity, because only then does the ΔG line cross zero.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate the plot as a clean conceptual graph rather than a data-heavy chart. Use a pink upper half and pale green lower half separated by a gray dashed ΔG = 0 line. The x-axis should read 'Increasing temperature (K)' and have no numeric scale; the y-axis should read 'Free energy' with only the zero tick labeled. Draw four thick diagonal lines starting at the left edge: red positive intercept with positive slope, green negative intercept with negative slope, yellow positive intercept with negative slope crossing zero, and yellow negative intercept with positive slope crossing zero. When a sign combination is selected, fade the other lines and labels, emphasize the selected line’s y-intercept, slope direction, and ΔG = 0 crossing if it has one. The temperature slider should display a vertical cursor and a highlighted dot on each visible line, colored or outlined according to whether the dot lies in the spontaneous or nonspontaneous region.

authoredContext:
Such a plot is shown in the figure. A process whose enthalpy and entropy changes are of the same arithmetic sign will exhibit a temperature-dependent spontaneity as depicted by the two yellow lines in the plot. Each line crosses from one spontaneity domain (positive or negative ΔG) to the other at a temperature that is characteristic of the process in question. This temperature is represented by the x-intercept of the line, that is, the value of T for which ΔG is zero:

So, saying a process is spontaneous at “high” or “low” temperatures means the temperature is above or below, respectively, that temperature at which ΔG for the process is zero. As noted earlier, the condition of ΔG = 0 describes a system at equilibrium.

These plots show the variation in ΔG with temperature for the four possible combinations of arithmetic sign for ΔH and ΔS.

A graph is shown where the y-axis is labeled, “Free energy,” and the x-axis is labeled, “Increasing temperature (K).” The value of zero is written midway up the y-axis with the label, “delta G greater than 0,” written above this line and, “delta G less than 0,” written below it. The bottom half of the graph is labeled on the right as, “Spontaneous,” and the top half is labeled on the right as, “Nonspontaneous.” A green line labeled, “delta H less than 0, delta S greater than 0,” extends from a quarter of the way up the y-axis to the bottom right of the graph. A yellow line labeled, “delta H less than 0, delta S less than 0,” extends from a quarter of the way up the y-axis to the middle right of the graph. A second yellow line labeled, “delta H greater than 0, delta S greater than 0,” extends from three quarters of the way up the y-axis to the middle right of the graph. A red line labeled, “delta H greater than 0, delta S less than 0,” extends from three quarters of the way up the y-axis to the top right of the graph.

discrepancies: the default view adds a vertical dashed temperature cursor and four colored circular sample points, which are not present in the static source figure and visually clutter the simple textbook diagram
the red upward line and green downward line are clipped by the top and bottom plot boundaries in the generated view, whereas the source shows their right ends remaining inside the plotting area

the zero line and temperature cursor both use dashed styling, making the source's single dashed ΔG = 0 boundary less visually dominant than it should be
evaluation.notes: The generated figure captures the thermodynamic sign-combination diagram well, but the default interactive cursor/points and slight endpoint clipping make it less like a clean drop-in replacement for the source.
action_items: Hide or greatly mute the vertical temperature cursor and sample points in the default state, revealing them only after slider interaction or in later demo steps.

Reposition the rotated ΔH/ΔS labels slightly away from the cursor sample points and enlarge them to better match the source label hierarchy.
Make the ΔG = 0 dashed horizontal line visually dominant compared with any optional vertical cursor line.
